**MEMO: Local AI Capacity — Buy More Hardware or Improve Utilisation?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** Recommendation on our local inference capacity decision
**Status:** For discussion at Thursday's planning session

Over the past quarter, our GPU utilisation has become the recurring topic in every retrospective. Our four local inference nodes sit idle most of the day, then saturate completely during batch runs and the afternoon development spike. The obvious question on the table is whether we should buy two additional nodes or invest in making better use of what we already own. I want to lay out my thinking ahead of Thursday, and I'll be direct: I believe we should improve utilisation first, and defer the hardware purchase by at least one quarter.

Let me start with the cost picture, because it's the least ambiguous part. Two additional nodes at current pricing would run us roughly £60,000 upfront, plus the incremental power, cooling, and maintenance overhead that our facilities team estimates at around £400 per month. That is not an impossible sum, but it is a meaningful fraction of our annual infrastructure budget, and it would crowd out other items we've been deferring, including the observability upgrade that several of us have argued is overdue. Improving utilisation, by contrast, is mostly an engineering time problem. A scheduling layer, better queueing for batch jobs, and a modest amount of work on model quantisation would consume perhaps six engineer-weeks. Even valuing that time generously, it is a fraction of the purchase price.

Latency is where the argument gets more interesting, and where I want to be honest about the trade-off. The case for more hardware is real: when all four nodes are saturated, interactive workloads queue behind batch jobs, and p95 latency for the internal assistant degrades from about 400 milliseconds to several seconds. That is a genuine productivity drag, and people feel it. But the latency problem is substantially self-inflicted. Our batch jobs currently run without preemption and without any priority classing, so a long-running fine-tuning job can block interactive traffic for an hour. Fixing that is not glamorous, but it attacks the actual symptom rather than buying our way around it. If, after we implement scheduling and priority classes, latency still degrades under normal load, then we will have learned something important and the hardware case becomes much stronger.

Reliability cuts both ways, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. More nodes means more redundancy: today, a single node failure removes a quarter of our capacity, and two simultaneous failures would be genuinely painful. That argument has real weight, particularly since our on-call rotation is thin and hardware failures tend to arrive at inconvenient moments. But I'd note that our current fleet has been stable, and the reliability benefit of additional nodes is speculative insurance against a failure mode we haven't yet experienced. Meanwhile, better utilisation practices — checkpointing batch jobs so they can be preempted, for instance — would actually improve our resilience to node failures today, because work in flight would survive interruption rather than being lost.

The opportunity cost consideration is, to me, the decisive one. Every pound and every engineer-week spent on new hardware is a pound and a week not spent on the product work that actually differentiates us. And hardware depreciates quickly in this space; the nodes we'd buy today will be unremarkable in eighteen months. Utilisation improvements, by contrast, compound: a good scheduling layer and disciplined queueing practices will make any future hardware we do buy more effective, because we'll have the tooling to use it well from day one.

Finally, reversibility. Buying nodes is a one-way door in practical terms — the capital is spent, the depreciation clock starts, and unwinding the purchase means writing off value. Improving utilisation is a series of reversible, incremental steps. If our scheduling work reveals that demand genuinely exceeds capacity even at high utilisation, we can still buy the nodes, and we'll do so with better data and better tooling. The reverse is not true: if we buy hardware and discover demand was never the constraint, we've locked in the cost.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. My utilisation estimates come from partial telemetry, and it's possible that our true peak demand is higher than the numbers suggest. If the scheduling work stalls or the telemetry shows sustained saturation above 80% even after these changes, I will happily reverse my position and sponsor the purchase request. What I'm proposing is not "never buy hardware" but "buy it later, with better evidence."

My recommendation: approve six engineer-weeks for the utilisation workstream, revisit the hardware decision at the end of next quarter with real utilisation data in hand, and hold the capital budget open in the meantime. I'd welcome pushback before Thursday — particularly from anyone who has felt the latency pain directly, since your experience is data I don't fully have.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Local AI hardware capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've been running into capacity ceilings on our local inference cluster more frequently over the past month. Queues for the fine-tuning jobs are stretching into the afternoon, batch inference windows are slipping, and two teams have asked whether they can "just get a few more cards." Before we commit budget, I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this decision, because I believe the right move is not the obvious one.

The case for buying more hardware is straightforward on its face. Our utilization data shows peak-hour saturation on the A100 nodes, and latency-sensitive workloads — the interactive inference endpoints our product teams depend on — are seeing p99 response times creep from 180ms toward 400ms during the midday crunch. That degradation is real and it's user-visible. Adding capacity would relieve it immediately, and hardware prices have softened enough that the per-FLOP cost of a new node is meaningfully better than what we paid eighteen months ago.

But the utilization picture complicates that story. When we look at the full week rather than peak hours, our cluster sits at roughly 45% average utilization. The problem isn't that we lack capacity in aggregate; it's that our capacity is badly shaped. Long-running fine-tuning jobs monopolize the high-memory nodes for hours, batch jobs are scheduled by hand rather than by a real queue, and interactive traffic shares hardware with workloads that could tolerate delay. In other words, we have a scheduling and isolation problem wearing the costume of a capacity problem. Fixing that — proper job queueing, workload tiering, dynamic batching on the inference path, and maybe moving a couple of batch pipelines to off-peak windows — would likely recover 20 to 30 percentage points of effective utilization at a cost of a few engineer-weeks rather than tens of thousands of dollars.

There's also the question of what we'd be giving up by buying. That capital is not free; it's the same pool of money that could fund an additional engineer, a vendor API budget for overflow, or simply extend our runway. And hardware depreciates fast in this field. The cards we'd buy today will be mid-tier in three years, and if the model landscape shifts — smaller efficient models, better quantization, or a move toward hosted inference for most workloads — we'd be holding an asset that's hard to repurpose. That's the opportunity cost argument, and I don't think we can wave it away.

Reliability cuts both ways, and I want to be honest about that. More nodes means more redundancy: today, a single node failure during peak hours takes down a meaningful fraction of our serving capacity, and that's a genuine operational risk. Improved utilization, by contrast, tends to make systems *less* forgiving — a tightly packed cluster has less slack to absorb failures or unexpected load spikes. If we go the optimization route, we need to preserve headroom deliberately, not squeeze it out. I'd propose we treat 70% sustained utilization as a ceiling, not a target.

On reversibility, the asymmetry favors optimizing first. Buying hardware is a largely one-way door: the money is spent, the depreciation clock starts, and if our needs change we're into the business of reselling used GPUs. Scheduling improvements, tiering, and queueing are all reversible — we can unwind them, adjust them, and learn from them cheaply. Sequencing the reversible move first buys us information. If, after a quarter of genuine optimization, we're still saturating at peak with a well-shaped workload, then the case for purchase becomes strong and evidence-based rather than speculative.

So my recommendation: hold off on hardware purchases for now. Fund a focused six-week effort on scheduling, workload isolation, and inference batching, with a clear success metric — p99 latency back under 250ms at peak, and sustained utilization above 60% without reliability regressions. Revisit the purchase decision in early Q3 with real data in hand. If we do end up buying, we'll know exactly how much capacity we need, and we may find that a smaller, cheaper purchase — or a hybrid arrangement with a cloud provider for burst capacity — covers the gap.

I acknowledge real uncertainty here. Utilization numbers can flatter; a cluster that looks 45% utilized on paper may be effectively full if the idle capacity is in the wrong shape or the wrong place. And engineer time is not free either — the optimization effort has a cost, and if it stalls, we'll have spent six weeks to learn what a purchase order would have told us in a day. That's a risk I'm willing to take given the asymmetry, but I want the team's eyes on it.

Let's discuss at Thursday's planning session. Please come with objections — especially from anyone with visibility into workloads I may have mischaracterized.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Engineering Lead
**Date:** Internal memo
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?

We've been running hot on our local inference hardware for a couple of months now, and the question on the table is whether we should purchase additional GPU capacity or invest in squeezing more out of the machines we already own. I want to lay out my thinking, make a recommendation, and be honest about where I could be wrong.

Let's start with the case that's easiest to make: utilisation. Our fleet telemetry tells a story we should not ignore. Peak-hour utilisation sits around 85 percent, which sounds alarming, but our average across a full week is closer to 40 percent. That gap is the whole problem in miniature. We have bursts of demand — batch embedding jobs, scheduled fine-tuning runs, the afternoon spike in interactive traffic — stacked on top of each other, and long stretches where expensive silicon idles. Buying more hardware to solve this would mean paying full price to fix a scheduling problem. Every serious attempt I've seen to model this suggests that better queueing, workload shaping, and moving batch jobs into off-peak windows could raise effective capacity by 30 to 50 percent without a single new purchase. The engineering cost is real — it's probably two to three weeks of focused work from one or two people — but it's a fraction of the capital cost of new cards, and it's work that pays off regardless of what we buy later.

On cost, the comparison is lopsided in another way too. New hardware is not just the sticker price. It's rack power, cooling, the operational burden of provisioning, and the depreciation of an asset that loses value quickly in a market where model architectures and hardware generations turn over every eighteen months or so. Utilisation work, by contrast, is labour we mostly already pay for, and the improvements compound: a better scheduler benefits any future hardware we do eventually buy.

Latency is the one place where the "buy more" argument has genuine force. Our interactive inference p99 has crept up during peak windows, and some of that is contention that scheduling alone cannot fully fix — if a large batch job is hogging memory bandwidth, the interactive request behind it suffers no matter how clever our queue is. I don't want to hand-wave this. User-facing latency is a product feature, and there's a real risk that optimisation work delivers average improvements while leaving tail latency stubbornly ugly. My answer to that is that we should first try the cheaper interventions — strict priority classes for interactive traffic, capping batch concurrency, possibly quantising or right-sizing models for the hot path — and measure. If p99 remains unacceptable after a genuine effort, that's strong evidence we have a true capacity ceiling, not a scheduling problem, and the case for buying becomes much stronger.

Reliability cuts both ways. More machines means more redundancy: today, a single node failure during peak hours degrades service noticeably, and that fragility is uncomfortable. But more hardware also means more components to fail and more surface area to operate. Better utilisation, done right, includes failover and load-shedding logic that improves resilience on the fleet we have. I'd rather build that muscle now and buy redundancy deliberately later, sized to a demand curve we understand, than buy capacity reactively because one Tuesday was painful.

Then there's opportunity cost, which I think is the most underappreciated factor. The engineers who would spend a month integrating and babysitting new hardware are the same people who could be shipping the batching and caching improvements that our users would actually feel. And capital spent on GPUs is capital not spent on the things we keep deferring — observability, the evaluation harness, the data pipeline work. Reversibility matters here too: an order for GPUs is largely irreversible once placed, while a scheduling and prioritisation project can be abandoned cheaply if it stalls. When one option is reversible and the other isn't, and the reversible one is also cheaper, the burden of proof belongs to the expensive one.

So my recommendation is this: commit the next six weeks to a utilisation push — workload shaping, priority scheduling, and honest measurement of tail latency — with a pre-agreed trigger. If, at the end of that window, peak p99 still violates our latency target or utilisation remains above 80 percent during business hours, we proceed with a hardware purchase, sized to the measured shortfall rather than to anxiety. That framing keeps us honest in both directions.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty explicitly. Our demand forecast is shaky; if the new product launch in Q3 drives traffic the way the business team hopes, we may hit a real ceiling faster than this plan assumes. The utilisation gains I've cited are based on our own telemetry and industry experience, not a guarantee. And there's a risk that the optimisation work turns out to be harder and more fragile than expected, in which case we'll have spent six weeks learning that we should have bought hardware — a cost I'm willing to accept, because that knowledge would have been worth having anyway.

I'd like to discuss this at Thursday's planning session. If there are objections, especially from anyone closer to the latency numbers than I am, I'd genuinely like to hear them before we commit.

— Engineering Lead
